sections.title: The General Rules of the Prohibitions of Kilayim and Their Reason
sections.html:
God created different species in the world, and in several matters He commanded us not to mix them with one another. As it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes: you shall not let your animals mate with a different kind; you shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed; and a garment of two kinds of material, sha'atnez, shall not come upon you." And it is stated (Devarim 22:9-11): "You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed, lest the full growth be forfeited, the seed that you sow and the yield of the vineyard. You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together. You shall not wear sha'atnez, wool and linen together." This prohibition is generally called 'kilayim', which means mixture. That is, although these are species each of which is permitted on its own, mixing them together is forbidden. Therefore the prohibition of cooking meat in milk is also included among the prohibitions of kilayim.

There are seven prohibitions of kilayim: 1) Kilei behema – not to mate two species of animals. 2) Not to work with two species of animals [together]. 3) Kilei ilanot – not to graft two species. 4) Kilei zera'im – not to sow two species of seeds together. 5) Kilei ha-kerem – not to sow grain and vegetables near grapevines. 6) Kilei begadim – not to wear garments in which wool and linen are mixed together. 7) Meat and milk.

The prohibition of kilayim applies to species of plants and animals. In some of the prohibitions of kilayim only the mixing is forbidden, but after the fact the result that emerges from the mixing is permitted for eating or benefit, as with kilei zera'im, kilei ilan, and kilei behema in mating and in work. And there are kinds of kilayim in which both the mixing is forbidden and what is produced from the kilayim is forbidden for benefit, as with kilei ha-kerem and cooking meat in milk. And with kilei begadim (sha'atnez), the prohibition is only to wear kilayim, but there is no prohibition to make it for gentiles or not for the purpose of wearing.

The mitzvot that are dependent on the soil, such as kilei zera'im and kilei ha-kerem, apply by Torah law in the Land of Israel only, throughout the borders of those who came up from Egypt (below 12, n. 2), whereas the mitzvot that are not connected to the soil, such as kilei begadim, meat and milk, and kilei behema – apply outside the Land as well. Kilei ilanot too, that is, grafting two trees onto each other, is forbidden outside the Land, since the prohibition is performed above the ground and not in the ground itself (below, section 5). Since the law of kilei ha-kerem is severe, in that they are forbidden to eat and for benefit, the Sages decreed to forbid them outside the Land as well (below 4:4).

Although we cannot understand the depth of the meaning of the mitzvot, which are Divine and whose root is above and beyond the human intellect, there are mitzvot whose reason we understand more, and they are called 'mishpatim' (ordinances), and there are those whose reason we understand less, and they are called 'ḥukim' (statutes). The mitzva of kilayim is among the ḥukim, about which it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes." And so Rashi explained, that they are decrees of the King that have no reason. One can explain that these statutes are the special characteristics that God implanted in all creatures, characteristics that point to the uniqueness and the destiny of each and every creature. And the Divine statute whose secret we cannot grasp is the understanding of the meaning and special destiny of each and every species that God created. And through the prohibition of kilayim we were warned to preserve the special and honored place of each species, not to blur its uniqueness by mixing it with another species (Ramban and Maharal there; Ḥinukh 244). And so the Sages said (Kiddushin 39a): "'You shall keep My statutes' – statutes that I already engraved for you (in the nature of creation) – you shall now keep."

Furthermore, in the interpretation of the word 'kilayim' there is the meaning of 'kele' (prison), for the mixing imprisons the characteristics of the species, so that it does not come to realization properly because of its mixing with the other species (Zohar vol. 3, 86a; Rabbeinu Baḥya). It is worth noting that with kilei zera'im and kilei ha-kerem, the prohibition already exists in their growing near each other, even though they themselves do not mix and merge; and their prohibition is in the Land of Israel, because in the Holy Land the Divine matter and His unity are revealed more, and consequently the uniqueness of each species is more recognizable, and one must preserve its special and honored place.1

sections.title: The Prohibition of Kilei Behema
sections.html:
It is forbidden to mate a male and a female of two species of animals, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes: you shall not let your animals mate with a different kind." And although it says "your animals" (behemtekha), the intention is all species of living creatures, including birds and the species found in the sea; and it says "your animals" as an example for the other species, because domestic animals are commonly found with man (Bava Kamma 54b). By Torah law it is forbidden to carry out the mating with one's own hands, that is, inserting "the brush into the tube" (inserting the male organ into the female's orifice). And the Sages added and forbade causing them to mate, for example by mounting the male onto the female in a way that causes them to mate. But there is no prohibition to put different species into one pen, and if they mate there is no need to separate them, since one did not perform an action that causes them to mate (SA YD 297:2-3).

Although there is a prohibition to mate two species of domestic or wild animals with each other, if one transgressed and mated a male of one species with a female of another species, it is permitted to benefit from the offspring. The most famous kilayim species is the mule (pered or pirda), born from mating a donkey with a mare. People did this because the mules born from mating a donkey and a mare are able to work well in carrying loads and in plowing. And since the prohibition is only to cause the birth of mules, it is permitted to buy mules and use them.

Mating two different species is forbidden, but two breeds of the same species is permitted. Therefore, it is permitted to mate bulls and cows of different breeds with each other, and likewise different breeds of sheep, or different breeds of cats or dogs. But two different species, even though they are relatively similar to each other, it is forbidden to mate. The definition of the species is determined according to the totality of the characteristics and form of each species (below, section 4). As a rule, one can say that the sign of two species is that they are unable to produce fertile offspring. Generally, from the mating of two species no offspring is born at all, and in the rare cases that one is born, as with a donkey and a mare, the offspring is sterile. And if we find two species that succeed in producing fertile offspring, apparently they are not two species but two types of one species, which there is no prohibition to mate with each other.2

sections.title: The Prohibition of Working With Two Animals of Different Species
sections.html:
In addition to the prohibition of mating two species with each other, the Torah forbade working with two different species together, for example plowing with an ox and a donkey together, or harnessing a wagon to a horse and a donkey. As it is stated (Devarim 22:10): "You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together." The Torah gave the example of an ox and a donkey because these are two domesticated species with which it is convenient to work, but the prohibition applies to any combination of two species of animals with each other for the purpose of work.3 Not only the wagon driver who harnesses the horse and the donkey to his wagon and directs their movement transgresses the prohibition, but anyone who assists in this. And even one who urges on the ox and the donkey with his voice, since he influenced them to pull the wagon or the plow onward – transgresses a Torah prohibition (SA YD 297:11; 13-14).

This prohibition was stated for Jews only. Therefore, if a Jew hired a gentile to transport his merchandise to another city, and the gentile decided to do so in a wagon harnessed to a horse and a donkey, there is no prohibition in this, since the Jew has no interest in this (Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 297:21). But a Jew is forbidden to sit in a wagon that a gentile drives with a horse and a donkey, because one who sits in the wagon becomes a partner in the work, for if he did not sit in the wagon, the driver would not command the animals to pull the wagon (SA there 12).

Only when the two species are tied together is there a prohibition of kilayim. Therefore, a person riding a horse is permitted to hold in his hand a rope tied to a dog. But it is forbidden to tie the dog's leash to the horse's saddle, for if he ties it, he joins them together, and sometimes the dog will get ahead of the horse and pull the horse forward, and he will thereby transgress the prohibition of kilei behema (Arukh Ha-shulḥan there 19).

As we learned, although we are unable to grasp the secret of the mitzvot, and especially of the ḥukim, the Sages of Israel endeavored to understand their reasons. The Rambam (Moreh Nevukhim 3:49) explained that this prohibition is intended to keep the different species apart from each other so that we do not stumble in the prohibition of mating a species with one not of its kind. And the Sefer Ha-ḥinukh (550) explained that the reason is so as not to cause them suffering. For each species loves to live with members of its own kind, whereas if it is joined with members of another species, it will suffer. And especially in work, for the strength of the domestic and wild animals of different species is not equal, and when they do not pull the wagon or the plow equally, they will suffer.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Grafting Trees
sections.html:
It is forbidden to graft two species of trees onto each other, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes: you shall not let your animals mate with a different kind; you shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed." Just as the intention is not to mate two species of animals with each other, so the intention of "you shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed" is not to graft two species of plants onto each other: neither trees of different species, nor vegetables of different species, and likewise not to graft a tree onto a vegetable or a vegetable onto a tree. Non-fruit-bearing trees are all considered one species; therefore it is forbidden to graft a fruit tree onto a non-fruit-bearing tree. But it is permitted to graft one non-fruit-bearing tree onto another, because all non-fruit-bearing trees are considered one species, for the characteristic of not yielding fruit is the principal one for this law, and it is what makes them all count as one species (SA 295:1-3; Rema 6).

This prohibition applies outside the Land as well, for although it seemingly is connected to the soil, in practice it is performed above the soil, and its action is similar to the prohibition of kilei behema, which is mentioned adjacent to it in the verse (Kiddushin 39a). Like the law of mating animals is the law of grafting trees: although the mating and the grafting are forbidden, what is produced from them is permitted ab initio for eating and for use.

The aim of grafting is to combine the good characteristics of two species or breeds of trees. For trees that yield many tasty fruits tend to have weak roots and to be infected by diseases and die, whereas strong and resistant trees generally give few and untasty fruits. To solve the problem, they are grafted onto each other. One plants in the ground a branch of a resistant tree, and it is called the 'kana' (rootstock). One cuts the rootstock in a special way, and onto it one attaches a branch from a tree with tasty fruits, which is called the 'rokhev' (scion). One binds the two parts together until they fuse, and so they continue to grow, with the roots and the beginning of the trunk belonging to the resistant species, and the continuation of the trunk, the branches and the fruits belonging to the species that yields many tasty fruits. In this way, although the two trees were grafted and joined, each part continues to function according to its natural characteristics. The rootstock connected to the ground operates its roots according to its nature, and the scion produces fruits according to its nature, so that there is almost no difference between the fruits growing on a scion grafted onto another species and a scion that grew naturally in the ground.

If the rootstock and the scion are of two different species, one who grafts them transgresses a Torah prohibition whose punishment is lashes. And if they are of different breeds of the same species, it is permitted to graft them onto each other. Therefore, it is permitted to graft a breed of large, red and sweet apple onto a breed of small, green and sour apple, since both are kinds of apples. But it is forbidden to graft a peach onto an almond, for they are two different species. The definition of a species with regard to kilayim is a broad definition; that is, the division of species is determined according to the totality of the tree's characteristics as it appears to our eyes, including the shape of the fruit, its taste, the tree's branches and leaves, and the nature of its growth. Therefore it is possible that certain trees will be considered by some people, or according to scientific classification, as two species, whereas according to halakha they will be considered one species. When the people of Israel lived on its land and the Great Sanhedrin decided every question and doubt, the tradition of the division of species with regard to kilayim was known and clear; however, over the course of time and with the many exiles, doubts arose regarding various trees that are difficult to resolve.4

sections.title: Grafting and Crossbreeding
sections.html:
The forbidden grafting of trees is the joining of two species of trees to each other in such a way that each part retains its characteristic, without any genetic merging between the two parts; however, crossbreeding a stamen and an ovary from two species is permitted. Every plant has a blossom, and in the blossom are male stamens and a female ovary, and by means of insects, butterflies and the wind the male pollen meets the ovary, and within it the female ovules, and through this the fruit is formed, in which is the seed from which another tree can grow. If male pollen is taken from a tree of one species and brought into contact with a female ovary of another species – a crossbreed of two different species will be created, and the fruit that grows will have genetic characteristics shared by both of its 'parents'. However, from each crossbreeding a somewhat different kind of fruit will emerge, for each time different components of the genetic sequence of each species will find expression, and thus a new combination will be created.

Generally, crossbreeding two species does not succeed, and the male pollen and the ovary do not merge and fertilize each other; and on the occasions when fertilization occurs, generally an unsuccessful fruit is produced. But sometimes the pairing succeeds and a fruit with a special taste is produced, or a tree with special qualities, for example that it is able to grow in a climate in which it previously could not survive. For this purpose many scientists labor to create all sorts of crossbreeds. And indeed there are rabbis who hold that just as it is forbidden to graft two species of trees onto each other, so it is forbidden to crossbreed them with each other (Shevet Ha-levi 9:224). However, the main halakhic view is that the Torah forbade only the act of grafting two different trees onto each other, in such a way that they live together contrary to the law of their nature, and not an act of crossbreeding, which is done even before the tree is formed. Furthermore, the pollen on its own is not a species, for it cannot grow on its own, and likewise the ovule in the ovary is not a species, and therefore there is no prohibition in crossbreeding them. All the more so there is no prohibition of grafting in genetic engineering, that is, in joining a component from one gene with another gene (and so is the opinion of Rav Yisraeli, Ha-Torah Ve-ha'aretz 3; Kerem Shlomo 2:1; Rav Ariel, Teḥumin 33).

sections.title: Benei Noaḥ and the Law of Kilayim
sections.html:
According to most of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, the prohibition of grafting trees and mating animals applies to Benei Noaḥ (gentiles) as well, even though it is not one of the 'seven Noahide laws'. For it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes," and the Sages learned from this: "Statutes that I already engraved for you" even before the giving of the Torah – "you shall keep." And as it is stated (Bereshit 1:12): "Vegetation, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, whose seed is in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good." From here we learn that these statutes obligate Benei Noaḥ as well (Sanhedrin 60a; She'iltot, Halakhot Gedolot, Rambam, Riaz, Gra, Arukh Ha-shulḥan and Rav Kook).

And some disagree and hold that there is no prohibition for Benei Noaḥ to graft trees or to mate different animals (Ritva, Rosh and Radbaz). But even according to them, a Jew is forbidden to ask a gentile to graft his tree or mate his animal. For just as a Jew is forbidden to ask a gentile to desecrate Shabbat for him, so he is forbidden to ask him to perform other Torah prohibitions for him with his property.

And it is possible that even according to the stringent opinion, the prohibition for Benei Noaḥ is only in a case where there is a clear and definite prohibition of grafting; but when there is a doubt whether it is a prohibition, for example perhaps the rootstock and the scion are of two breeds of one species, there is no prohibition for them (see Mishpat Kohen 13).5

sections.title: Is It Permitted to Plant and Maintain a Grafted Tree?
sections.html:
As we learned, although it is forbidden to graft two species of trees onto each other, the fruits growing from the grafting are permitted ab initio. The question is whether, after people transgressed and grafted two trees, it is permitted to tend the grafted seedling and water it so that it will grow. This question is very practical. For example, among pear trees most of the trees are grafted in a forbidden manner, and likewise among plum and peach trees there is a high frequency of trees grafted in a forbidden manner; and the question is whether it is permitted to plant a seedling that was grafted in a nursery in a forbidden manner, and if it has already been planted, whether it is permitted to tend it or whether one must uproot it.

Some hold that the prohibition is to graft two different species, but from the moment the grafting has been done, there is no longer a prohibition to maintain the grafted tree; and if a grafted seedling was prepared in a nursery, it is even permitted to plant it in the field and tend it. This is because the law of grafting trees is similar to the law of kilei behema, where the prohibition is only to mate an animal of one species with another species, but afterward it is permitted to raise the animal that was born and to use it.

However, according to many poskim it is forbidden to maintain a grafted tree (SA YD 295:7). But they disagree about the meaning of the prohibition: some say that one who has a grafted tree in his field is obligated to uproot it; and some say that it is forbidden to uproot the weeds around it and to prune it in order to improve its growth, but it is permitted to leave it in the field without care. And some say that the prohibition of maintaining a grafted tree applies only until the stage at which the rootstock and the scion fuse, but after that it is permitted to maintain the grafted tree and even to plant it.

In practice, some rely on the lenient approach, that the entire prohibition is only to graft, but afterward, even though the graft has not yet fully fused – it is permitted to plant the grafted seedling, maintain it and tend its growth. However, according to halakha, the opinion of most poskim is that it is forbidden to maintain the grafted seedling until the time of its fusion, but after that there is no prohibition to plant it and tend it. And ideally it is good to follow the stringent opinion, and even after the graft has fused not to tend a grafted tree; but where there is a doubt whether its grafting was done in a forbidden manner from two separate species or was done in a permitted manner from two breeds of the same species, one may be lenient to maintain it and tend it.

One who buys a fruit tree must clarify that the tree was not grafted in a forbidden manner, for even according to the lenient authorities who hold that it is permitted to plant a grafted seedling, one who buys from someone who grafts in a forbidden manner assists transgressors. And since the law is complex, one may rely in this only on a God-fearing seller who is knowledgeable in the laws or who is under reliable supervision regarding kilayim.6
